title: Finetuning CLIP to Reason about Pairwise Differences

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to address the lack of structural properties (e.g., vector arithmetic analogies) in CLIP's embedding space and improve reasoning about pairwise image differences. Paper [1] explicitly identifies the same problem: "A notable drawback of CLIP... is that the resulting embedding space seems to lack some of the structure of its purely text-based alternatives. For instance, while text embeddings... satisfy analogies in embedding space using vector arithmetic, CLIP has no such property." This matches the stated purpose at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves synthesizing textual descriptions of image differences using an LLM on image-caption pairs, then fine-tuning CLIP with a contrastive loss to align image embedding differences with these textual embeddings. Paper [6] introduces a similar mechanism for Image Difference Captioning (IDC): "The Image Difference Captioning (IDC) task aims to describe the visual differences between two similar images with natural language... we propose a new modeling framework... leveraging pre-training and contrastive learning." Both approaches use synthesized textual descriptions of image differences and contrastive learning to align embeddings, making the underlying primitive equivalent.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves testing PC-CLIP on difference-based classification tasks (e.g., sorting paired images by attributes like size or color) and measuring accuracy improvements. Paper [13] uses a similar evaluation design for fine-grained visual comparisons: "Given two images, we want to predict which exhibits a particular visual attribute more than the other... we propose a local learning approach for fine-grained visual comparisons." Both papers evaluate models on pairwise attribute-based classification tasks, making the evaluation design equivalent.

### Domain
The domain is vision-language models, specifically CLIP fine-tuning. Paper [1] operates in the same domain: "Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP are trained via contrastive learning between text and image pairs... useful for many downstream tasks." This contribution does not introduce a new application area but rather refines CLIP within the established vision-language domain.

Papers like [4], [5], and [6] evaluate prompt-based methods for vision-language models on downstream classification tasks, including comparisons with baseline methods (e.g., CLIP). These prior works use similar evaluation designs (benchmark subsets, performance comparisons, and hyperparameter tuning), making the evaluation facet covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of vision-language models and reasoning tasks. Papers such as [4], [5], [6], and [9] also address vision-language models and their adaptation to downstream tasks, including classification. The domain is therefore covered.

#### Purpose:
The contribution's purpose is to validate that differential fine-tuning can simultaneously introduce new capabilities without harming standard zero-shot classification, and that the gains specifically arise from the comparative information itself. None of the prior papers explicitly establish this empirical relationship. The use of standard benchmarks and metrics for zero-shot classification is not novel.

This domain is extensively covered by prior papers such as [2], [3], [4], [7], [8], and [18], which all work within the general application area of vision-language models and their fine-tuning or zero-shot capabilities.
